**Understanding the problem**

An integer m divides n when n = k * m for some integer k; we must decide whether n has exactly three positive divisors. Divisors pair up as (d, n / d) with product n, so the count is usually even; an odd count forces a perfect square, whose root pairs with itself.

Examples:
- n = 2: divisors 1 and 2 -> count 2 -> false.
- n = 4: divisors 1, 2, 4 -> count 3 -> true.

With n <= 10^4 even a full scan to n works, but scanning only to sqrt(n) - or exploiting the structure behind having exactly three divisors - is cleaner and generalizes better.
k: A number has exactly three positive divisors if and only if it is p * p for a prime p: its divisors are 1, p and p * p.
While enumerating divisor pairs up to sqrt(n), count a perfect-square root once rather than twice.
n = 1 has just one divisor, so any solution must reject it explicitly.

a.n: Approach 1: Trial Division up to sqrt(n)
a.i: Every divisor d <= sqrt(n) is paired with n / d >= sqrt(n), so scanning d = 1, 2, ... while d * d <= n discovers all divisors: add 2 per hit, except add 1 when d * d == n because the root pairs with itself. Comparing the tally with 3 settles the question directly.
s: For d = 1 while d * d <= n: if n % d == 0, add 2, or 1 when d * d == n.
a.t: O(sqrt(n)) - one pass up to sqrt(n)

a.n: Approach 2: Perfect Square of a Prime
a.i: An odd divisor count forces n = r * r, whose divisors are 1, r and r * r; these are three distinct values exactly when r is prime. Compute r = floor(sqrt(n)), reject when r * r != n or r < 2, then trial-divide r up to sqrt(r) to confirm primality.
s: Take r = floor(sqrt(n)); return false if r * r != n.
Return false if r < 2 (this rejects n = 1).
For i = 2 while i * i <= r: return false if i divides r.
a.t: O(n^(1/4)) - the primality loop only scans to sqrt(r) <= n^(1/4)

w: Open with the p * p characterization - it signals number-theory fluency - and keep the sqrt-scan as a safe fallback for these constraints. Pitfalls: accepting n = 1 as 1 * 1 (its root is not prime), and double-counting the square root. Follow-up: count how many integers below N have exactly three divisors - enumerate primes p with p * p <= N.
